title: This year in the science of learning
author: Holly Korbey
summary: Korbey's 2025 year-end post maps what readers engaged with most and signals where the science-of-learning movement is heading. The free portion (detailed retrospective is paywalled) traces the year through five diagnostic pieces: critiques of NCTM's math position paper ignoring learning evidence, fragmented curriculum review sites with no focus on actual outcomes, retrieval practice reframed as more than quizzing, reports of bare shelves in popular reading curricula, and Kansas's success building LETRS-style math training at scale. The framing argument is sharp: a year ago Korbey opened the same post acknowledging almost nothing concrete on implementation at scale; now she launches a Science of Learning Tracker mapping adoption across states, districts, and schools, signaling the early-adopter era is closing and the next phase is about whether implementation can stay honest to evidence as scale grows.
points: The science-of-learning movement is moving from early adoption to scaled implementation; what matters now is whether schools can stay faithful to the evidence as practice spreads.
Popular curricula are still misaligned with what research says about learning, from NCTM position papers ignoring cognitive load to reading programs offering few whole books.
Retrieval practice has been liberated from rote learning association and recognized as inseparable from thinking itself, signaling a maturation in how the field talks about evidence.
Fragmentation in curriculum review creates choice paralysis for leaders; no single organization centers on which programs produce reliable learning results.
State-level adoption of evidence-based professional development for teachers (like Kansas's LETRS math training) is rare and worth noting as a signal of breakthrough scale.
quotes: I sent 71 newsletters, conducted 11 video/podcast interviews, wrote seven Tools for Practice posts with the help of very smart educators, hosted one summer reader book club (a blast) and one live Q&A with readers and Paul Kirschner, a giant in the science of learning.” “I launched the Science of Learning Tracker, which is going to give readers an idea of where the science of learning is being implemented, whether it’s states, universities, districts or schools.

Earlier this year, a position paper published by the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics highlighted suggestions for improving math teaching, but few of them were based in evidence of how students learn.

The organizations that review curricula to help leaders choose what is best for students is piecemeal and confusing, my reporting showed, with each organization coming up with its own criteria and none of them focused on which programs produced reliable learning results for students.
Retrieval practice is not the “glorified path to rote learning.” It’s a lot more than quizzing, it’s the key to thinking, according to the research.
Some of the U.S.’s most popular reading curricula, including Wonders, feature either very few whole books, or none at all, across elementary grades.

There’s little right now in terms of data: we don’t know how many teachers know about ideas like cognitive load theory or working memory; we don’t have data on how many teachers understand the research behind how humans learn. In the U.S. anyway, it’s just too early to know. If you are reading this, you are an early-adopter…
Now, in only a year, that’s beginning to change.” Archived from The Bell Ringer (Substack) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
